# Volume 4 — CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

Upon opening her eyes on the morning she was to be married, Nell saw the sunlight glimmering through the window in the small porch gable while a breeze of September played about her curtains.
{: #nw-v04-c04-p0000 }

“It makes me so happy that the sun’s rays will fall upon me,” was her joyful thought.
{: #nw-v04-c04-p0001 }

Nell remembered her initial morning waking inside that small porch room, as sunbeams slithered in toward her past the old Frost Maiden's drifting blossoms. That wakefulness had lacked joy, bringing alongside itself the preceding night's sharp letdown. Yet over the intervening time, years filled with joyful childhood daydreams and young womanly reveries had made the tiny chamber beloved and hallowed. Following every time she was away, she had returned to it with delight; beside its pane she had dropped to her knees during that night filled with sharp anguish when she thought Hugh was passing away, and beside it she had remained seated in silent bliss during the evening she became engaged. Numerous watchful nights of gladness along with a few of grief had occurred inside; and on this day she was required to abandon it eternally. From this point forward it would not belong to her; fifteen-year-old Lucy was destined to receive it once she departed. Neither did Nell desire a different outcome; the tiny chamber belonged sacredly to youth and maidenhood—to that former time slated to end on this day prior to the start of her story as a wife.
{: #nw-v04-c04-p0002 }

Grey Shutters became a bustling and happy home during that morning. Isolde came early, accompanied by little Gideon and Small Nell Lucinda, so that she could assist. Robin and Lucy, who were the Grey Shutters twins, carried the babies away to the garden.
{: #nw-v04-c04-p0003 }

“Make sure Small Nell Lucinda doesn’t ruin what she’s wearing,” Isolde cautioned with concern.
{: #nw-v04-c04-p0004 }

“You do not have to fear leaving Lucy in her care,” Thirza said. “That youngster possesses greater sense and caution than the majority of mothers I have encountered. In certain respects, she is truly remarkable. She bears little resemblance to the other reckless one I raised.”
{: #nw-v04-c04-p0005 }

Thirza offered a smile to Nell over her chicken salad. One could even imagine that the wild creature was her favorite, when all was said and done.
{: #nw-v04-c04-p0006 }

“The twin children are truly lovely,” Mrs. Agatha remarked, once she was certain they could no longer hear her. “Lucy shows such helpfulness and mature grace, while Robin is growing to be quite a clever lad. He has ceased being the dreadful little troublemaker he was in the past.”
{: #nw-v04-c04-p0007 }

“I have never felt as bewildered in my entire life as I did during his initial six months with us,” Thirza admitted. “Following that period, I imagine I became accustomed to his presence. Recently, he has developed a keen interest in agriculture and desires my permission to attempt managing the farm in the coming year. I might allow it, since Mr. Pembroke does not believe he will wish to lease it for much longer, necessitating a different plan.”
{: #nw-v04-c04-p0008 }

“Well, Nell, the weather for your wedding is certainly lovely,” Isolde stated while pulling a large apron across her silk attire. “Even if you had ordered it from Eaton’s, you could not have gotten a better one.”
{: #nw-v04-c04-p0009 }

"In truth, that exact company, Eaton's, receives far too much money from this Island," declared Mrs. Sowerby crossly. Expressing her firm opinions regarding predatory department stores was a habit she indulged whenever possible. "Furthermore, the Brierley girls treat those catalogues like the Bible nowadays, and that is a fact. Rather than reading the Holy Scriptures on Sundays, they scrutinize those books instead."
{: #nw-v04-c04-p0010 }

“Indeed, for entertaining young ones, they are wonderful,” Isolde remarked. “The illustrations keep Gideon and Small Nell occupied for hours.”
{: #nw-v04-c04-p0011 }

“Without using Eaton’s catalogue, I entertained a total of ten children,” Mrs. Agatha stated sternly.
{: #nw-v04-c04-p0012 }

“Come on, you two, do not fight about Eaton’s catalogue,” Nell said cheerfully. “You know, this is the most special day I have ever had. Because I am so glad, I wish for all other people to be glad as well.”
{: #nw-v04-c04-p0013 }

“I’m sure I hope your happiness will last, child,” sighed Mrs. Agatha. Indeed, she truly hoped for it and possessed faith in it, yet she held a fear that displaying one's joy with too much openness amounted to provoking Providence. For her own benefit, Nell needed to be moderated just a bit.
{: #nw-v04-c04-p0014 }

Yet the bride who descended the old, homespun-carpeted staircase that September noon was joyful and lovely—the initial bride of Grey Shutters, slim and bright-eyed, wrapped in the mist of her bridal veil, holding an armful of roses. Hugh, who was awaiting her in the hallway beneath, gazed up at her with adoration in his eyes. She belonged to him finally, this elusive, long-pursued Nell, earned following years of steadfast waiting. It was toward him she was approaching in the gentle yield of a bride. Was he deserving of her? Would he be able to render her as joyful as he desired? Should he fail her—should he fall short of her ideal of manhood—then, as she extended her hand, their glances locked and every uncertainty was wiped out by a joyful confidence. They were meant for one another; and, regardless of what the future might bring them, that could never be changed. Their joy was entrusted to each other, and neither felt any fear.
{: #nw-v04-c04-p0015 }

They were wed in the bright sunlight of the ancient orchard, surrounded by the affectionate and friendly faces of lifelong companions. Mr. Wace performed the marriage, and the Reverend Ez offered what Mrs. Agatha Sowerby later declared was the “most beautiful wedding prayer” that had ever met her ears. Although birds rarely sing during September, a songbird warbled sweetly from a concealed branch as Hugh and Nell spoke their immortal vows. Nell listened to it and felt a thrill; Hugh listened to it, feeling surprised only that every bird on earth had not broken into triumphant song; Cedric listened to it and subsequently composed a poem about it that became one of the most praised pieces in his initial collection of poetry; Belinda the Fourth listened to it and felt joyfully certain it boded good fortune for her beloved Miss Harcourt. That bird continued its song until the service reached its end, concluding with a single wild, happy little trill. The old gray-green dwelling surrounded by its enveloping orchards had never experienced a brighter, happier afternoon. Every traditional joke and witticism that must have served at marriage celebrations since the time of Eden was brought out, appearing just as fresh, clever, and amusing as though they had never previously been spoken. Mirth and happiness reigned supreme; and as Nell and Hugh departed to make the Delford train, driven by Cedric, the twins stood prepared with rice and worn shoes, which Belinda the Fourth and Mr. Pettifer assisted gallantly in tossing. Thirza remained at the gate, observing the carriage until it disappeared down the lengthy lane bounded by goldenrod. At its extremity, Nell turned to wave her final farewell. She had departed—Grey Shutters was no longer her residence; Thirza’s countenance appeared exceedingly gray and aged as she walked back toward the dwelling that Nell had supplied with illumination and vitality for fourteen years, even when she was away.
{: #nw-v04-c04-p0016 }

However, Isolde along with her young children, the inhabitants of Echo Cottage, and the Waces remained behind so that the two elderly women would not feel lonely on their initial night; moreover, they managed to enjoy a calmly delightful small supper, remaining at the table for a extended period and discussing every single detail regarding the day. At the time they were seated there, Nell and Hugh were stepping off the train in Glen St. Agnes.
{: #nw-v04-c04-p0017 }
